newsitem.title: UK: Cross winds chill dlr/yen, warm dlr/mark in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Cross winds chill dlr/yen, warm dlr/mark in Europe.

text.p: The dollar was pulled in opposite directions in late Europe as mark/yen bore the brunt of a resurgent Japanese currency.

Dollar/yen, which struggled to recover in Europe after diving overnight to 117.50 -- six yen down from Friday's high -- surrendered the spotlight to the cross and watched the mark slice below 70 yen to its weakest levels in almost a year.
Dollar/mark, however, shook off a weak European start to climb the best part of two marks on the day.
Though some Japanese officials tried earlier to curb the yen, traders said current market sentiment was against them.

"I think we'll consolidate for a couple of days, but I think the trend is still downwards for dollar/yen and eventually for dollar/mark and dollar/Swiss too," said Richard Hill, head of FX trading at Bank of America in London.

A senior official of Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party said on Monday that changing Japan's record low rates would undermine the economy. Taku Yamasaki, head of the LDP's policy research council, also said a dollar/yen level of around 120 would be appropriate.
The dollar was quoted at 118.70 yen at 1537 GMT, way down from Friday's late European level of 120.05/20.
Eisuke Sakakibara, the influential Japanese finance official who floored dollar/yen last week with his mention of a possible rate of 103, said the dollar was likely to "settle down soon".
Analysts said Japanese officials had repeatedly expressed concern over the yen's "excessive" weakness during the dollar's recent rally, but were startled at the speed of the correction.

"The Japanese can't just turn around and say excessive moves are undesirable only in one direction... so they made a rather weak statement showing that they are really quite happy with this sort of level," said Francis Breedon, foreign exchange economist at Lehman Brothers.
Mark/yen plunged to a low of 69.67 yen before edging back to 69.75/80 by 1603 GMT. That was well below Friday's close of 71.42/47 and more than 2-1/2 yen below Friday's session high.

"The mark/yen move is probably the preferred move for the authorities," said Standard Chartered treasury economist Tim Fox. "The Japanese are happy with a stronger yen and the Germans are reasonably happy with a weaker mark against the yen."
Dollar/mark firmed to 1.7030/40 marks by 1604 GMT from late Friday's European level of 1.6863/68. It had fallen as low as 1.6680 marks in Asia overnight, according to Bank of Japan data.
The dollar stumbled briefly against the mark around European midsession after a Bundesbank council member said a further rise in its value could cause a price problem in the long term.
Reimut Jochimsen said the dollar's recent drop would not hurt German exporters and said he would be disturbed if dollar/mark "shot through the roof".
No U.S. data were released on Monday, but the market was awaiting April retail sales out on Tuesday as the first in this week's batch, which includes producer and consumer prices.
Anything which dampens speculation of U.S. tightening could hit a dollar already undermined by Japanese rate hike talk.
"The markets will be looking for the data to substantiate their view of no change in (U.S.) rates," said StanChart's Fox.

U.S. Federal Reserve policymakers meet on May 20 to decide whether to change rates. Fed chairman Alan Greenspan puzzled players last week with ambiguous comments on the economy, but the overall feeling was that a May 20 hike looked less likely.

Elsewhere, sterling leaped two pfennigs in late Europe after finance minister Gordon Brown said Britain had no plans to rejoin Europe's exchange rate mechanism. But he also said two-year membership of the ERM was not essential for EMU participation.
-- Abigail Levene, London Newsroom +44-171-542-8968
